idiom_name: val + scala.collection.immutable with structural sharing + case class copy
implementation_notes: Scala's default collections are immutable - collections in scala.collection.immutable are guaranteed never to change, and update-looking operations return a new collection that shares structure (List prepend shares the whole tail; Vector is a wide trie with effectively constant-time index and update) - so whole-structure copies are unnecessary. val fixes the binding and case class generates copy as the wither; collections in scala.collection.mutable exist for local accumulation and are converted (toVector, toList) before a value escapes, and mutable state is confined to a builder or var inside one method. Immutability is what makes sharing between threads, actors and cached versions safe. The classic hand-written immutable type is still justified when state must be hidden behind an interface: keep the fields in a case class and expose only transformation methods.
code_sketch:
case class Config(name: String, ports: Vector[Int]):
  def withPort(port: Int): Config = copy(ports = ports :+ port)  // new Config; receiver unchanged

val base = Config("api", Vector(8080))
val next = base.withPort(8443)
// List prepend shares the tail; Vector updates share the trie structure
pitfalls: val only fixes the reference: val xs = scala.collection.mutable.ArrayBuffer(...) still lets every holder mutate the collection in place.
Arrays are mutable and compare by reference: a case class with an Array component gets identity equality and a broken hashCode, so use Vector/List/ArraySeq and convert at the edges.
Choosing the wrong immutable collection gives quadratic behaviour: List append and indexing are O(n) while Vector is effectively constant - prepend with +: on List, index with Vector.
copy() is shallow: a nested mutable object, Iterator or resource is shared with the previous version.
